mark_split.label: Identify the reciprocal class and the root −1
Divide the quotient by x² and put x + 1/x = t

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.22 — LAQ chapter 2 Theory of Equations, answer 13. Printed appearances: TS 15, 17 · AP 16, 17. THE MARK SPLIT IS THE BOOK'S, with one division of ours inside it: the page prints [2 Marks] beside the synthetic division / 'now we solve the SRE' block, then [1 Mark] against the substitution, the t values, t = 3, t = −5/2, and the final list of roots (2+1+1+1+1+1 = 7). The card splits the printed 2 as 1 (identify the class and the root −1) + 1 (the synthetic division), so that the two ideas can be recalled separately. The SAME step ids (s1_identify, s2_divide, s3_substitute, s4_solve_t, s5_first_t, s6_second_t, s7_roots) are used on answers 13, 14 and 15, deliberately: one method — remove the root ±1 by synthetic division, then solve the standard reciprocal quotient with x + 1/x = t. The per-step MARKS differ across the three because each page prints its own [N Marks] tags and the card follows its page; a step that the page does not mark separately carries 0 and no red mark. The book writes the substitution letter as y; the card writes t. The book's chapter header carries ★★★; that star is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's. Paper position: Maths-2A Section C runs Q18–Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q19 is the Theory of Equations slot (blueprint, book p.3; all five model papers pp.111–120 agree). The Bullet Model Paper re-solves this question under Q19 on book p.105 — arithmetic cross-checked, identical. Correction to the book, recorded not silently fixed: in the printed synthetic-division table on p.22 the last entry of the middle row reads 2; it must be −2 (2 × (−1)), which is what makes the remainder 0 — the book's quotient and roots are unaffected. Truth check: f(−1) = 0 by substitution; the five roots add to −1 − 2 − 1/2 + 3 = −1/2 = −a₁/a₀. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. No two-book check and no board back-test exist for this paper (no second Maths-2A source in the corpus; answer-book/papers/ holds first-year physics only) — recorded, not hidden.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — which root you take out first and why, how you divide, and how the quotient is solved with t = x + 1/x.
insider_note: The last mark is for listing all five roots; the root −1 removed at the start is the one most often left out of the box.

steps.label: Class I, odd degree
steps.margin_note: First mark (the book prints a single [2 Marks] over this step and the next). Odd degree, coefficients 2, 1, −12, −12, 1, 2 equal from both ends: class I, odd degree, so −1 is a root. Substitute to confirm.
lines: Degree n = 5 is odd, and aₖ = aₙ₋ₖ for every k
So this is a reciprocal equation of class I
and odd degree; x = −1 is always a root of it.

recall.must_convey: That the equation is a reciprocal equation of class I and odd degree, so x = −1 is a root for certain, and that this is confirmed by substitution (f(−1) = 0).
accept: it is a reciprocal equation of class I and odd degree so −1 is a root, check it by substituting
the coefficient pattern tells you −1 is a root before you do anything else
first note that x equals −1 satisfies the equation because of the reciprocal pattern
idi class I and odd degree reciprocal equation, kabatti −1 root avutundi, substitute chesi check cheyyali
the reciprocal class gives the root −1 with no extra work, verify by putting it in

steps.why: For a reciprocal equation the roots come in pairs x and 1/x. A root that is its own reciprocal must be 1 or −1, and the class (whether aₖ equals aₙ₋ₖ or −aₙ₋ₖ) together with the parity of the degree tells you which of them the equation must contain. Naming it costs one line and saves a whole degree.
common_mistakes: Reading the class from only the first and last coefficients instead of every pair.
Naming the wrong one of ±1 as the root (class I odd gives −1, class II gives +1).
Not substituting the root back to confirm it, which the examiner expects to see.

steps.label: Divide by (x + 1)
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Synthetic division by −1: bring down 2, multiply by −1, add, repeat. The last entry must be 0. The quotient 2x⁴ − x³ − 11x² − x + 2 is itself reciprocal (2, −1, −11, −1, 2).

recall.must_convey: That the polynomial is divided by (x + 1) by synthetic division, with zero remainder, leaving the quotient 2x⁴ − x³ − 11x² − x + 2, which is again reciprocal.
accept: divide by (x + 1) using synthetic division, the remainder is zero and the quotient is a reciprocal quartic
synthetic division by (x + 1) brings the degree down to four
take out the factor (x + 1) by synthetic division and keep the quotient
(x + 1) tho synthetic division chesthe remainder zero, quotient reciprocal quartic vasthundi
remove the known root by dividing and work with the quotient

steps.why: The known root is removed by division so that what remains is a STANDARD reciprocal equation of even degree, the only kind the t-substitution handles. Synthetic division also proves the root, because the remainder comes out 0.
common_mistakes: A sign slip in the synthetic division row, so the remainder is not 0 and the quotient is wrong.
Writing the quotient with one coefficient too many or too few (degree must drop by exactly 1 per division).
Dividing by (x − 1) when the root is −1, or the reverse.

steps.label: Put x + 1/x = t
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Divide the quotient by x², group, and substitute. 2(t² − 2) = 2t² − 4, and −4 − 11 = −15.
lines: Put x + 1/x = t, so x² + 1/x² = t² − 2

recall.must_convey: That the quotient (a standard reciprocal quartic) is divided by x², and x + 1/x = t with x² + 1/x² = t² − 2 turns it into a quadratic in t.
accept: divide the quotient by x squared, put x plus one by x equal to t, and the squared pair is t squared minus two
the quartic quotient is reciprocal so divide by x square and substitute t
group the quotient into x squared plus one by x squared and x plus one by x then put t
quotient ni x square tho divide chesi x plus one by x ni t ga pettali, t square minus two vasthundi
the quotient becomes a quadratic in t after the substitution

steps.why: The quotient is even-degree and symmetric, so dividing by x² pairs each term with its matching term from the other end and the identity x² + 1/x² = t² − 2 turns four powers of x into one quadratic in t.
common_mistakes: Writing x² + 1/x² = t² and losing the −2.
Forgetting to multiply the leading coefficient into the −2.
Substituting in the ORIGINAL equation instead of the quotient.

steps.label: Solve for t

recall.must_convey: That the quadratic in t is factorised (or solved) to give the two values of t.
accept: factorise the quadratic in t and get the two values of t
solve the t equation by splitting the middle term
the quadratic in t factors and gives two t values
t quadratic ni factorise chesi rendu t values teeskovali
split the middle term of the t equation and read off t

steps.why: The t-equation is a plain quadratic, so factorising it is the cheapest way to the two values of t. Each t value will give two x values, so the count of roots (2 × 2 = 4) is checked here before any x is found.
common_mistakes: A sign slip when splitting the middle term.
Stopping at the two t values as if they were the roots.
Solving the t-quadratic with the formula and making an arithmetic slip a factorisation would have avoided.

steps.label: t = 3
steps.margin_note: Fifth mark. x² − 3x + 1 = 0 has discriminant 9 − 4 = 5; the roots stay as surds.

recall.must_convey: That t = 3 is put back into x + 1/x = t, multiplied out to a quadratic in x, and solved to give the roots (3 ± √5)/2.
accept: put t equals 3 back so x plus one by x is 3 multiply by x to get a quadratic and solve it
x plus one over x equals 3 gives a quadratic in x whose roots are (3 ± √5)/2
go back from t equals 3 to a quadratic in x and solve
t equals 3 ni tirigi x plus one by x lo petti quadratic solve cheyyali
multiply x plus one by x equals 3 through by x and use the quadratic formula

steps.why: Each value of t gives two values of x, because x + 1/x = t is a quadratic in x. Solving both t values is what recovers all 5 roots of the original equation — stopping at t answers a different question.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply through by x, so the equation in x is never formed.
A slip inside the square root: 9 − 4 = 5.
Not simplifying the surd form of the roots at the end.

steps.label: t = −5/2
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. Multiply x + 1/x = −5/2 by 2x: 2x² + 5x + 2 = 0 factorises as (2x + 1)(x + 2). The book reads −5/2 = −2 − 1/2 straight off; same roots.

recall.must_convey: That t = −5/2 is put back into x + 1/x = t, multiplied out to a quadratic in x, and solved to give the roots −2 and −1/2.
accept: put t equals −5/2 back so x plus one by x is −5/2 multiply by x to get a quadratic and solve it
x plus one over x equals −5/2 gives a quadratic in x whose roots are −2 and −1/2
go back from t equals −5/2 to a quadratic in x and solve
t equals −5/2 ni tirigi x plus one by x lo petti quadratic solve cheyyali
multiply x plus one by x equals −5/2 through by x and use the quadratic formula

steps.why: Each value of t gives two values of x, because x + 1/x = t is a quadratic in x. Solving both t values is what recovers all 5 roots of the original equation — stopping at t answers a different question.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply through by x, so the equation in x is never formed.
A slip inside the square root: 2x² + 5x + 2 factorises as (2x + 1)(x + 2), no formula needed.
Not simplifying the surd form of the roots at the end.

steps.label: All five roots
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Five roots for a degree-5 equation: −1 from the division, −2 and −1/2 from t = −5/2, and the surd pair from t = 3. Their sum is −1/2 = −a₁/a₀.

recall.must_convey: That all 5 roots are listed together — the root(s) removed by division AND the roots found through t: −1, −2, −1/2 and (3 ± √5)/2.
accept: list all 5 roots together, the one taken out at the start and the ones from t
the roots are −1, −2, −1/2 and (3 ± √5)/2
do not forget the root removed by division when writing the final answer
anni 5 roots ni kalipi raayali, modata teesina root tho paatu
the final answer collects the roots from both parts of the working

steps.why: The equation was split into a linear factor and a quotient; its roots are the roots of BOTH pieces. The final line is where the removed root is most often forgotten, so it is written out with the others.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the root removed by synthetic division.
Listing the t values among the roots.
Writing a ± pair as one root and so reporting too few roots.
